No Tax on Tips 2026: Who Qualifies, the $25,000 Limit, and the Full Occupation List

Direct AnswerNo tax on tips is a federal deduction of up to $25,000 for 2025–2028. See who qualifies, the full 71-occupation list, phase-outs, and how to claim it.

"No tax on tips" is real — but it is a deduction, not an exemption. For tax years 2025 through 2028, workers in 71 listed occupations can deduct up to $25,000 of qualified tips. Tips are still reported as income, still owe Social Security and Medicare tax, and your paycheck is unchanged during the year — your final federal income-tax bill is not.

As the technical tools architect at Hourly Wage Converter, I build the calculators tipped workers use, and this is their most-asked tax question. This guide pulls the whole rule set into one place: who qualifies, what counts, the full 71-occupation list, the phase-out, worked examples, and how to claim it.

The Short Answer: A Deduction, Not a Free Pass

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed July 4, 2025, added a deduction (IRC Section 224) for “qualified tips.” The headline and the reality differ in four ways:

  • It is a deduction, not an exemption. You report all tips as income, then deduct up to $25,000 when you file. Your saving is the deduction times your marginal rate — not the full $25,000.
  • Federal income tax only. Social Security and Medicare tax (7.65%) still applies; state rules vary.
  • It is temporary. Tax years 2025–2028 only, unless Congress extends it.
  • It is occupation-based. Only tips earned in one of the 71 listed occupations qualify — see the full list below.

It is a sibling of the overtime deduction in our no-tax-on-overtime guide: same window, same claim-at-filing design. Earn both, and the two deductions stack.

Who Qualifies: Every Rule in One Place

Five gates stand between you and the deduction:

Requirement The rule
Occupation Your job is on the IRS list of 71 occupations that customarily and regularly received tips before December 31, 2024
Qualified tips Voluntary tips in cash or cash equivalents, received directly or through a tip pool, reported on a W-2, a 1099, or Form 4137
The cap Up to $25,000 per return per year — a married couple shares one cap, even if both earn tips
Income phase-out Shrinks by $100 per $1,000 of modified AGI over $150,000 ($300,000 joint); gone at $400,000 ($550,000 joint)
Filing rules A Social Security number must be on the return; married taxpayers must file jointly — married filing separately cannot claim it

Two edges catch people out. First, the phase-out shrinks the deduction itself: at $180,000 of modified AGI, a single filer's maximum falls by $3,000, to $22,000 — and it reaches zero at $400,000. Second, self-employed workers face an extra limit — the deduction cannot exceed the net income of the business the tips came from.

What Counts as a Qualified Tip (and What Does Not)

A qualified tip passes three tests: it is paid in cash or a cash equivalent, the customer chose it freely, and it lands on an information return. The IRS final regulations draw the lines like this:

Counts as a qualified tip:

  • Cash, credit and debit card tips, checks, gift cards, and electronic payments
  • Tips received through a tip pool — including back-of-house staff such as dishwashers and cooks
  • Screen tips, as long as the customer could reduce the amount to zero
  • Amounts paid on top of a mandatory charge, for the portion above it

Does not count:

  • Mandatory service charges and automatic gratuities. An 18% charge on a large party's bill is wages, not a tip, even if passed to staff
  • In-kind gifts — tickets, meals, or merchandise are not cash tips
  • Digital assets. Cryptocurrency tips are excluded under the final regulations
  • Amounts paid by your own employer, or where you hold a significant ownership interest in the paying business — presumed to be recharacterized wages
  • Tips received in a specified service trade or business (health, law, accounting, performing arts, athletics) or tied to illegal activity
  • A manager's or supervisor's tip-pool share. Direct tips for their own service in a listed occupation can qualify; pool shares cannot

The Full Occupation List: All 71 Jobs in 8 Groups

Every qualifying job carries a Treasury Tipped Occupation Code (TTOC). The 2025 proposal listed 68 occupations; the final regulations added three — visual artists, floral designers, gas pump attendants — for 71. What matters is the work you do, not the industry label:

Category Qualifying occupations
Beverage and Food Service (10) Bartenders; wait staff; food and beverage servers, non-restaurant; dining room and cafeteria attendants and bartender helpers; chefs and cooks; food preparation workers; fast food and counter workers; dishwashers; host staff (restaurant, lounge, and coffee shop); bakers
Entertainment and Events (11) Gambling dealers; gambling change persons and booth cashiers; gambling cage workers; gambling and sports book writers and runners; dancers; musicians and singers; disc jockeys (except radio); entertainers and performers; digital content creators; ushers, lobby attendants, and ticket takers; locker room, coatroom, and dressing room attendants
Hospitality and Guest Services (4) Baggage porters and bellhops; concierges; hotel, motel, and resort desk clerks; maids and housekeeping cleaners
Home Services (9) Home maintenance and repair workers; home landscaping and groundskeeping workers; home electricians; home plumbers; home heating and air conditioning mechanics and installers; home appliance installers and repairers; home cleaning service workers; locksmiths; roadside assistance workers
Personal Services (10) Personal care and service workers; private event planners; private event and portrait photographers; private event videographers; event officiants; pet and show animal caretakers; tutors; nannies and babysitters; visual artists; floral designers
Personal Appearance and Wellness (11) Skincare specialists; massage therapists; barbers, hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists; shampooers; manicurists and pedicurists; eyebrow and eyelash technicians; makeup artists; exercise trainers and group fitness instructors; tattoo artists and piercers; tailors; shoe and leather workers and repairers
Recreation and Instruction (6) Golf caddies; self-enrichment teachers; recreational and tour pilots; tour guides and escorts; travel guides; sports and recreation instructors
Transportation and Delivery (10) Parking and valet attendants; taxi and rideshare drivers and chauffeurs; shuttle drivers; goods delivery people (including app and platform delivery); personal vehicle and equipment cleaners; private and charter bus drivers; water taxi operators and charter boat workers; rickshaw, pedicab, and carriage drivers; home movers; gas pump attendants

If your job is not on this list, your tips do not qualify — even if customers tip you daily. Some entries surprise people: dishwashers and cooks qualify because tip pools count; digital content creators qualify for voluntary viewer payments, but not for payments that buy access.

How Much You Save: Worked Examples

A deduction saves tax at your marginal rate, so the same $25,000 is worth very different amounts:

Qualified tips deducted Saved at 10% Saved at 12% Saved at 22% Saved at 24%
$10,000 $1,000 $1,200 $2,200 $2,400
$15,000 $1,500 $1,800 $3,300 $3,600
$25,000 (the cap) $2,500 $3,000 $5,500 $6,000

Example 1 — the full-time server. Maria earns $21,000 in wages and $13,500 in reported tips, all qualified, so she deducts $13,500. At her 12% marginal rate that saves about $1,620. Her tips still owed 7.65% Social Security and Medicare tax — roughly $1,033 — untouched by the deduction.

Example 2 — two tipped spouses. Devon, a bartender, reports $19,000 of tips; his spouse Priya, a hairstylist, reports $12,500. Together that is $31,500 — but the cap is $25,000 per return, so they deduct $25,000, worth about $3,000 at their 12% rate. The shared cap is the deduction's most common disappointment for tipped couples.

Example 3 — the gig driver. A rideshare driver receives $8,400 in tips and nets $36,000, so the full $8,400 is deductible. Had net income been $7,000, the deduction would cap at $7,000 — and the tips would owe self-employment tax either way.

Your saving ≈ qualified tips deducted × your marginal tax rate

Example: $13,500 of tips × 12% = about $1,620 saved; at the cap, $25,000 × 22% = $5,500. To see the paycheck those tips ride on, try our Paycheck Calculator.

How to Claim It: Reporting, W-2s, and Your Return

The deduction lives and dies on reporting: tips that never reach a W-2, a 1099, or Form 4137 do not qualify:

  • Track tips daily. Keep a daily tip diary (Form 4070A). App and card tips are captured automatically; cash is where records matter.
  • Report tips to your employer monthly. Employees report tips of $20 or more per month (Form 4070 or the employer's system), so the year-end W-2 matches the diary.
  • Check your year-end forms. For 2025, employers could show cash tips in Box 14 or on a separate statement (with IRS penalty relief). From 2026, W-2s separately report qualified cash tips and your TTOC code. Gig workers use their 1099s and platform records.
  • Claim it on your federal return. Deduct the qualified amount (up to $25,000, after any phase-out) on Form 1040, itemizing or not. Tips never reported to an employer go on Form 4137.

Set this expectation now: your paycheck does not change during the year. Withholding and the full 7.65% FICA continue as before; like the overtime deduction in Is Overtime Taxed at a Higher Rate?, the benefit arrives at filing.

State Taxes: Your State May Not Follow

The deduction is federal; whether your state copies it depends on how it ties its code to Washington's:

  • Rolling-conformity states adopt federal changes automatically, so the deduction generally flows through — Oregon and North Dakota give tipped workers the break on both returns.
  • States with their own versions. New York added its own exclusion of up to $25,000 from tax year 2026; Colorado kept the tips deduction while dropping the overtime one; Michigan and Indiana enacted limited versions.
  • Decoupled states. Illinois and Georgia require an add-back, so tips stay fully taxable at state level; California has signaled it will not adopt it.
  • No-income-tax states (Alaska, Florida, Nevada, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington, Wyoming) make the question moot.

State positions were still moving through 2026, so confirm your state's current rule before assuming the saving doubles. Our paycheck tax guide shows where state tax fits in a pay stub.

Frequently Asked Questions About No Tax on Tips

Straight answers to the questions tipped workers ask most:

Is no tax on tips really tax-free?

Not exactly. It is a federal income-tax deduction of up to $25,000 of qualified tips, claimed when you file for 2025–2028. You still report every tip, tips still owe Social Security and Medicare tax, and withholding continues as before — the benefit arrives as a smaller bill or a bigger refund.

Who qualifies for the no tax on tips deduction?

Workers in one of the 71 occupations on the IRS list who receive voluntary cash tips reported on a W-2, a 1099, or Form 4137. You need a Social Security number on your return, must file jointly if married, and stay under the phase-out starting at $150,000 of modified AGI ($300,000 joint).

Do cash tips count, or only card tips?

Both count — cash, checks, card tips, gift cards, and electronic payments, including tip-pool shares. What does not count: mandatory service charges and automatic gratuities (wages, not tips), in-kind gifts, and cryptocurrency tips.

Can I claim the tips deduction if I take the standard deduction?

Yes — whether you itemize or take the standard deduction. It reduces taxable income by up to $25,000 of qualified tips.

Does no tax on tips apply to self-employed and gig workers?

Yes, if your occupation is listed — rideshare and delivery drivers are the classic example. One extra limit: the deduction cannot exceed the net income of the business the tips came from. Tips still owe self-employment tax.

Will my state also stop taxing my tips?

It depends. States that automatically follow federal changes generally let it flow through; a few passed their own versions — New York added a matching exclusion from 2026. Others, including Illinois and Georgia, require an add-back.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

A valuable break — with more conditions than the slogan suggests. The plan:

No Tax on Tips: Summary Checklist

  • Check your occupation first: Only the 71 listed jobs qualify; if yours is not listed, no tip is deductible.
  • Report every tip: Unreported tips cannot be deducted. Keep a daily log, especially for cash.
  • Know your real saving: Deducted tips × your marginal rate — $3,000 at 12%, $5,500 at 22%, at the cap.
  • Watch the shared cap: Two tipped spouses split one $25,000 limit; married filing separately gets nothing.
  • Expect nothing mid-year: Withholding and FICA continue as usual; the saving arrives with your refund.
  • Check your state separately: Some copy the break, some add it back, nine never taxed tips.

Rules follow Internal Revenue Code Section 224, added by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (signed July 4, 2025), and the IRS final regulations published April 13, 2026 (effective June 12, 2026), which set the 71-occupation TTOC list, the $25,000 cap, and the $100-per-$1,000 phase-out over $150,000 ($300,000 joint) of modified AGI. Savings figures are illustrative marginal-rate math, before state taxes and credits. State notes reflect 2026 guidance. This article is general education, not personal tax advice.
